Title: Thermoluminescence - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
Thermoluminescence (TL) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating have become widely used in Quaternary studies. In one such example, TL dates from late Pleistocene loess successions in eastern Washington, USA, indicated that the ages of tephra inter-beds were significantly older than those implied by earlier 14C dating, suggesting a much longer eruptive history (>50 ka) for Mount St. Helens than previously accepted (Berger and Busacca, 1995; Fig. 17). Tephra ages have also been determined by TL dating of bracketing loess from sites in Alaska (Berger et al., 1996), Aotearoa-New Zealand (Berger et al., 1992), and Japan (Watanuki et al., 2005). Beyond the ∼55-ka limit to 14C dating, TL and OSL dating can potentially provide an extension into the late Quaternary where methods based on radioactive decay (40Ar/39Ar, K/Ar, U-decay series and fission track) can be applied for comparison. One of the most comprehensive multi-method comparisons was applied to Rangitawa Tephra (Pillans et al., 1996)—a 350-ka marine and terrestrial inter-regional tephra marker bed in Aotearoa-New Zealand dated by luminescence, fission track (glass and zircon), K/Ar, Ar/Ar methods and orbital tuning (Fig. 18). Thermoluminescence (TL) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating have become widely used in Quaternary studies. Tephra ages have also been determined by TL dating of bracketing loess from sites in Alaska (Berger et al., 1996), New Zealand (Berger et al., 1992), and Japan (Watanuki et al., 2005). Beyond the ~ 60-ka limit to 14C dating, TL and OSL dating provide an extension into the late Quaternary where methods based on radioactive decay (K/Ar, U-series, and fission track) can be applied for comparison. One of the most comprehensive multimethod comparisons was applied to Rangitawa Tephra (Pillans et al., 1996) – a 350-ka marine and terrestrial interregional tephra marker bed in New Zealand dated by luminescence, fission track (glass and zircon), K/Ar, Ar/Ar methods, and orbital tuning (**Figure 17**). Both TL and OSL measurements are made on mineral grains extracted from the material to be dated, for example, pottery or sediment. Traditional OSL and TL techniques used multiple grains to measure trapped signal during burial (e.g., Huntley et al., 1985) (Figure 10(A4)).

results.title: Contingency Plans for Project Risk Management: A Guide
results.content: # What are the most common contingency plans for managing project risks? Contingency plans are essential for managing project risks, especially when dealing with uncertain or complex situations. A contingency plan is a predefined course of action that can be implemented if a risk event occurs, to minimize its impact on the project objectives. In this article, you will learn about the most common types of contingency plans for project risk management, and how to create and use them effectively. Before you can develop contingency plans, you need to identify and analyze the potential risks that could affect your project. In project management, contingency plans for managing risks include identifying and analyzing potential risks, prioritizing them based on severity and likelihood, and categorizing them into types such as technical, operational, financial, legal, or environmental. Effective communication and documentation involve maintaining a risk register, keeping stakeholders informed, and training the project team on executing contingency plans. Depending on the risk response strategy you choose, you may need to develop one or more of the following types of contingency plans. In instances surfing in VUCA environments, where risks are difficult to identify, aside of contingency reserves for known and identified risks, better to setup enough Management and Schedule reserves to be able to respond to unforeseen risks, which can arise easily, in such way to allow continue with project work ensuring reaching project goals. Developing effective contingency plans requires a systematic process, which begins by defining the scope and objectives of the plan and aligning them with the project goals and stakeholder expectations. The roles and responsibilities of the contingency plan team should be identified and assigned to the appropriate project members or external parties. The contingency plan should then be integrated with the project plan, updating the project schedule, budget, and risk register accordingly. ## 5 Contingency Plan Use. To utilize contingency plans effectively, you should review and update them regularly to reflect any changes in the project environment, assumptions, or risks. Contingency plans are useful for managing project risks and improving project performance and success.

How much sample of volcanic rock is required to undertake a K-Ar date measurement, and does it matter if the rock contains vesicles? * $\begingroup$ In answer to the first question I suspect it depends on your instrument although I've never done it myself. * $\begingroup$ Are you dating whole rocks? What are the K contents of your rock? You need to ask the people who are going to date your rock what they need and how much of it. ## 1 Answer 1. I run an argon lab which does also K-Ar measurements. The sample amount depends on the age because you need enough signal strength to measure the radiogenic argon component precisely. Young rocks have very low 40Ar\* and to get enough volts on the detector you need more sample. For K measurements 30 mg in our lab is routine. For the argon measurement we usually use about 2 mg; for very young rocks up to 200mg for rocks with ca. We can date volcanic rocks of less than 20000 years using this technique and have dated historic eruptions successfully in our lab. Usually customers can say if the rocks are very young, so I usually prepare the sample amount accordingly. Regarding sampling technique itself- look for minerals with more potassium, such as muscovite, biotite, amphiboles, or more felsic rocks. I also have to say that Ar/Ar is a more accurate tool for most rocks and minerals, and then just a few mg is enough if the samples are Mesozoic or older. If they are very young, higher sample amounts are required as with the K-Ar technique. * $\begingroup$ Can you give a quick outline of the possible "false positive" or "false negative" conditions for K-Ar dating? 40Ar/39Ar dating on a trachyte of this caldera yields upper pleistocene ages of 449 ± 7 Ka. Some extracalderic formations like basaltic trachy-andesites and trachybasalts yield some Ar/Ar ages from 279 ± 3 Ka to 219 ± 3 Ka. A trachytic pumice sample of the "Vallée du Telluromètre" (northern limit of the "Dôme Carva" volcano-complex) is much younger with an Ar/Ar age of 26 ± 3 ka (Gagnevin and al., 2003). Another datation on a trachyte of this volcano-complex yields very young Ar/Ar ages around 10 Ka.
